clue.text: Directions announced for seamstress and farmer somewhere in London

parts.note: the directions are spoken orders, one word each, to the two workers that follow

indicators.note: what is announced is heard, so the letters come from the sound of the words

parts.note: the instruction you give a seamstress is 'Sew!'
the instruction you give a farmer is 'Hoe!'

explanation.surface: Someone shouts out orders to a seamstress and a farmer, somewhere in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Directions' is not compass points here but commands: 'Sew!' for the seamstress, 'Hoe!' for the farmer. Soho is a district of central London.
explanation.definitionFit: Soho is a district in London's West End, so it is somewhere in London.

clue.text: Dresses cut outrageously — for this one?

definitions.text: Dresses cut outrageously — for this one?

indicators.note: outrageously means wildly, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: A question about who wears dresses cut in a daring, revealing way.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: a seductress is the sort who wears outrageously cut dresses. The dash and question mark flag the double reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A seductress is the woman for whom a daringly cut dress would be chosen.

clue.text: Duke included in inquiry about health? The nerve!

indicators.note: what is included in something sits inside it

parts.note: first part of 'How are you?', the everyday question about someone's health
D is the abbreviation for duke
the rest of 'How are you?'

explanation.surface: A duke is asked how he is feeling and takes offence at the cheek of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About health' belongs to the inquiry, not to a reversal or container; it simply tells you the question is 'How are you?'.
explanation.definitionFit: 'How dare you!' and 'The nerve!' are both indignant exclamations at someone's cheek.

clue.text: This may show you a rainbow meandering for certain

definitions.text: This may show you a rainbow

indicators.note: something meandering wanders about, so the letters move out of order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: A promise that a winding path will certainly lead you to a rainbow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For certain' looks like padding meaning 'definitely', but it supplies every letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A rainbow appears when sunlight is refracted, bent and split, by raindrops.

clue.text: Carries out belongings

definitions.meaning: to effect a plan is to carry it out
the plural noun for what a person owns, used in wills and police property bags

explanation.surface: Someone carries their belongings out of a house.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a phrase, 'carries out belongings' is a removal; split in two, it is a verb and a noun that share one spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Effects is both a verb meaning carries out and a noun meaning personal possessions.

clue.text: Contemptible sort oversees conveniences for motorists (but not residents)

parts.note: a rat is a contemptible person
to run a business is to oversee it

explanation.surface: A despised official is in charge of roadside facilities for drivers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conveniences' suggests public toilets; here it is shortcuts. A rat run is a side street drivers use to dodge main-road traffic, to the annoyance of people living there.
explanation.definitionFit: Rat runs are handy for drivers cutting through, and a nuisance to the residents of those streets.

clue.text: What may be seen all around Lancashire?

definitions.text: What may be seen all around Lancashire?

parts.words: What may be seen all around
parts.note: surface reading: something visible everywhere; setter's reading: a wrapping that goes round the outside of something
surface reading: the English county; setter's reading: the crumbly cheese named after it

explanation.surface: A question about something visible everywhere in the county of Lancashire.
explanation.walkthrough: Lancashire reads as the English county; it is the crumbly cheese named after it, traditionally matured wrapped in cheesecloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheesecloth is the loose cotton gauze wrapped all around a cheese such as Lancashire.

clue.text: Everyman had to take on assistant, one dealing with email etc

parts.note: the setter, Everyman, refers to himself as I; I had = I'D
PA = personal assistant
the 'd of I'D, short for had

explanation.surface: The setter complains he had to hire an assistant to deal with his email.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter's name in a clue means I or ME; here 'Everyman had' is I'D, which takes PA inside.
explanation.definitionFit: An iPad is a tablet computer, a device you deal with email and the like on.

clue.text: Nightingale's wings in site of literary murder

indicators.note: a bird's wings are at its sides, so take the letters at each edge of the word

parts.note: the left-hand edge of NIGHTINGALE
the right-hand edge of NIGHTINGALE

explanation.surface: A nightingale's feathers turn up at the scene of a crime from a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The wings here are two letters each, not one. The literary murder is Agatha Christie's Death on the Nile.
explanation.definitionFit: Agatha Christie's Death on the Nile sets its murder on a steamer on the river.

clue.text: Organiser of libraries said to be somewhat wet

indicators.note: what is said is spoken, so the answer sounds like the name

parts.note: Melvil Dewey devised the Dewey Decimal system for shelving library books

explanation.surface: A librarian is described as a bit damp.
explanation.walkthrough: The organiser is Melvil Dewey, whose Dewey Decimal Classification numbers the shelves in libraries worldwide.
explanation.definitionFit: Dewy means covered in dew, lightly moist.

clue.text: No longer enjoying Pink Floyd album? Crazy

parts.note: to go off something is to stop liking it
The Wall is Pink Floyd's 1979 album

explanation.surface: Someone who has gone off a Pink Floyd record calls it mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crazy' sits after the question mark as a separate verdict, so the definition is at the end, not with the album.
explanation.definitionFit: Off-the-wall means bizarre or unconventional, near enough crazy.

clue.text: Scarce enough to manage? Take a new approach

indicators.note: to manage letters is to handle and arrange them into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

explanation.surface: If supplies are only just sufficient to get by, a change of plan is needed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scarce enough to manage' reads as a complaint about rations; every letter of 'scarce enough' is in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom from sailing and flying: altering your heading, used figuratively for adopting a different plan.

clue.text: Fidgety recluse agog, seeing Hollywood big-shot

indicators.note: something fidgety cannot keep still, so the letters shift about

parts.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

explanation.surface: A restless hermit is thrilled to meet a film mogul.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a hermit starstruck by a mogul; the mogul is made of the hermit's own letters.
explanation.definitionFit: George Lucas created Star Wars and is one of Hollywood's most powerful filmmakers.

clue.text: Had fun? Noted

definitions.meaning: to celebrate is to have a party
noted as an adjective: famous, well known

explanation.surface: A question and a curt reply: did you enjoy yourself? Point taken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noted' looks like a verb, 'I have written that down'; it is the adjective, famous.
explanation.definitionFit: Celebrated is the past tense of celebrate, making merry, and an adjective meaning famous.

clue.text: Gentle swab for treatment somewhere in India

indicators.note: what is sent for treatment gets worked on, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: A doctor uses a soft swab to treat a patient somewhere in India.
explanation.walkthrough: The medical surface makes 'for treatment' look like part of the story; it tells you to rework 'gentle swab'.
explanation.definitionFit: West Bengal is a state in eastern India, capital Kolkata.

clue.text: Footwear? They've got cloven hooves!

definitions.meaning: Reebok is a brand of trainers
the reebok, or rhebok, is a small South African antelope

explanation.surface: Asked what is on their feet, someone jokes that they have hooves.
explanation.walkthrough: The trainer brand took its name from the antelope, so the two definitions are the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: A trade name for the first sense; for the second, the Afrikaans-derived name of a small grey South African antelope, also spelt rhebok.

clue.text: Hide in quarter of Greek island?

parts.note: SE, south-east, is a quarter of the compass
Crete is the largest Greek island

explanation.surface: Someone goes into hiding in one district of a Greek island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it puts one thing inside another; here it only joins the definition to the wordplay, and 'quarter of' is a compass point placed before the island.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to conceal, from the same Latin root as secret.

clue.text: Caretaker sent back copper and silver vessels

indicators.note: what is sent back returns the way it came, so the letters run right to left

parts.note: a copper is a penny coin, abbreviated P
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
pots are vessels

explanation.surface: A caretaker returns some copper and silver containers.
explanation.walkthrough: Copper here is the coin, not Cu. Caretaker means a temporary stand-in, as in a caretaker manager.
explanation.definitionFit: A caretaker manager or government is a stopgap, filling in until a permanent one arrives.

clue.text: Guide is glib, high-flying type

parts.note: a pat answer is glib, too ready
a tern is a seabird

explanation.surface: A tour guide is dismissed as smooth-talking and ambitious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High-flying type' suggests a go-getter; it is literally a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A pattern is a model or template to guide you, as in dressmaking.

clue.text: It might be some homework, Chuck

definitions.meaning: a piece of schoolwork done over weeks, often at home
as a verb: to throw, hurl or cast forward

explanation.surface: A parent tells a child named Chuck that this could be homework.
explanation.walkthrough: Chuck looks like a boy's name being addressed; it is the verb, to throw.
explanation.definitionFit: Project is both a school assignment and a verb meaning to hurl.

clue.text: A printmaker has these urges

definitions.meaning: the machines a printmaker squeezes inked plates onto paper with
to press someone is to urge them

explanation.surface: An artist who makes prints is said to have strong impulses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Urges' reads as a noun after 'has these'; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Presses are the machines a printmaker uses, and presses means urges.

clue.text: Fashionista puts on bridle, saddle, etc?

definitions.meaning: a person who loves dressing up and showing off the latest fashions
read the answer as a verb and its object: dresses the animal in its tack

explanation.surface: A fashion lover tries on horse tack.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads the answer as a verb and object: someone who clothes a horse puts on its bridle and saddle. The question mark flags the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: A clothes horse is a person devoted to dressing fashionably.

clue.text: Lamb and Teddy regularly tucked up

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so take every other letter

parts.note: second and fourth letters of lAmB
second and fourth letters of tEdDy

explanation.surface: A child's toy lamb and teddy bear are tucked up in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' only joins the two words; the even letters are taken from Lamb and Teddy separately.
explanation.definitionFit: Abed means in bed, tucked up for the night.

clue.text: Sport unleashing mammoth opponents, primarily?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so take the first letter of each word before it

parts.note: first letters of Sport, Unleashing, Mammoth, Opponents

explanation.surface: A sport that sets huge opponents loose on each other.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: sumo is the sport of enormous wrestlers.
explanation.definitionFit: Sumo is Japanese wrestling between very heavy opponents.

clue.text: Conservative: I'm ready for my photo and something to eat

parts.note: blue is the colour of the UK Conservative party
'Cheese!' is what you say to smile for the camera

explanation.surface: A Tory politician poses for a photo and wants a snack.
explanation.walkthrough: In British politics the Conservatives are blue, so a Conservative is a Blue.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: blue-veined Stilton or Roquefort is one kind of food.

clue.text: Male host, agreeable — to some extent

indicators.note: only part of the words is used, so the answer lies within them

parts.note: hoSTAGreeable

explanation.surface: A man hosting a party is fairly pleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash sets off the indicator; the answer runs across the comma from 'host' into 'agreeable'.
explanation.definitionFit: Stag means for men only, as in a stag party.

clue.text: Lethargy resulting from some heated rows in Essex

indicators.note: only some of the words is used, so the answer lies within them

parts.note: heateDROWSINESSex

explanation.surface: Arguments in Essex leave everyone worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: Essex is an English county east of London; here it only supplies the letters ESS.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both name the heavy sluggishness of someone about to nod off.

clue.text: Behold: Detective Inspector's flipping hero

indicators.note: what is flipped is turned over, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: lo! is an old word for behold
DI is the abbreviation for Detective Inspector

explanation.surface: Look: the police inspector is a hero, and a bloody one at that.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British swear word, as in 'flipping hero'; its job is to reverse LO DI.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a pop or sporting idol is looked up to as a hero.
